newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives attack Labour on schools policy.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives attack Labour on schools policy.

text.p: The Conservative party announced on Wednesday an expansion of a scheme to help children from poorer families attend independent schools as part of an attempt to highlight its differences with Labour over education policy.

Junior education minister Cherly Gillan told reporters more than 200 independent schools would share 1,200 new assisted places. These include 118 preparatory schools, a sector that is joining the Assisted Places Scheme (APS) for the first time.

The expansion will help fulfil a commitment made by Prime Minister John Major in October 1995 to double the size of the APS -- a scheme Labour has said it will scrap to pay for its pledge to reduce primary school class sizes to no more than 30.
Labour has moved closer to the Conservatives on key aspects of schools policy such as national testing and the need to raise classroom standards and weed out poor teachers.
But with education shaping up as one of the central issues of the coming election campaign, the Conservatives are keen to talk up the remaining differences.
As well as the APS, these include Labour's pledge to scrap the government's fledgling nursery vouchers scheme and its plans to check that independent schools merit their charitable status.
Education Secretary Gillian Shephard, flanked by Gillan at a news conference, said Labour's education policy was driven by "innate, class-envious hostility".

Shephard said: "Labour hate choice and opportunity, unless of course it's choice and opportunity for their own children. All would go under Labour: grammar schools, grant-maintained schools, nursery vouchers, assisted places, and much more."

Gillan seized on a magazine article by Labour education spokesman Peter Kilfoyle in which he said independent schools would be safe under a Labour government but that it would want to be sure such schools had earned their charitable status.
Gillan accused Labour of seeking to abolish independent schools by the back door -- a charge hotly denied by Kilfoyle.
"There is no threat to the charitable status of those many many schools which operate according to their charitable objectives -- no threat at all," Kilfoyle told Reuters.
But he said it was right that a responsible government should look again at the status of schools if they were designated as charitable institutions centuries ago but had since become very wealthy.
"If you have something that is claiming to be a charity but which is not operating within the terms on which charitable status is based, then it's unacceptable," he said.
